subsection: 10. Case study: the Montgomery bus boycott, 1956

notes.h: Background: Jim Crow, discrimination and the NAACP
notes.b: By 1955 black Americans in the South lived under a legal system of racial separation. Montgomery's buses were one everyday place where that system was enforced, and it is the setting for the whole case study.
points: Discrimination means treating people unequally because of their race. In the South it was not just prejudice but the law: Jim Crow laws (state and local laws enforcing racial segregation) kept black and white people apart in public places, which is why a bus seat could become a legal issue.
The legal basis was the Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson ruling of 1896, which upheld 'separate but equal' facilities. In practice this meant that segregation worked as discrimination.
Black Americans in the South were largely excluded from voting, so they had little power to change the laws through elections. This is why they turned to the courts and to protest.

The NAACP (the national organisation that fought segregation through the courts, with local branches in cities such as Montgomery) was the main legal weapon. Its branch leaders, Rosa Parks and E. D. Nixon among them, later shaped the boycott.
The black church was the main institution free of white control, since ministers did not depend on white employers for a living. This made the churches the natural base for organising protest.

The Supreme Court's Brown v. Board of Education decision of May 1954 ruled school segregation unconstitutional. It raised black hopes, and it also hardened white resistance: the White Citizens' Councils, which began in Mississippi in 1954, spread across the South and were committed to resisting any change.
There is more on this in the notes on racial conflict and the civil rights movement.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to separate the long-term causes (segregation, the exclusion of black voters, the NAACP and the churches) from the trigger, which was the arrest of Rosa Parks. Keep these apart in an essay.

notes.b: Montgomery, the state capital of Alabama and the first capital of the Confederacy, enforced bus segregation by city ordinance and by Alabama state law. Because black people were the large majority of riders, the rules were a daily grievance for most of the city's black population.
points: Buses reserved the front rows for white passengers and the rear for black passengers. The driver could move the dividing line backwards to make room for white riders, so black passengers were made to stand or give up their seats.
Black passengers had to pay at the front and then get off and re-enter by the rear door. Drivers often insulted black riders or drove off before they re-boarded.
Drivers had police powers under the city code, which meant a black passenger who argued with a driver could be arrested. This is why refusing to move a seat was a legal offence, not just rudeness.
Black riders made up the large majority of passengers, so the rules affected most of the city's black working population. Many were maids and labourers who rode to work in white homes and businesses.
This also explains why a boycott could work: if black riders stayed off the buses, the bus company would lose most of its income.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level, learn the basics: Montgomery, Alabama, and the front-for-white, rear-for-black seating. One correct fact earns a mark.

notes.b: The December 1955 boycott did not appear from nowhere. Black activists in Montgomery had already warned of a boycott and had already been trying to find the right person to challenge the law.
points: The Women's Political Council (WPC), a group of black women founded in Montgomery in 1946 and led from 1950 by Jo Ann Robinson, wrote to Mayor W. A. Gayle in May 1954 warning of a boycott. So the WPC was ready to act.
In March 1955 Claudette Colvin, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat. In October 1955 Mary Louise Smith, aged eighteen, was arrested on the same charge.

Local leaders including E. D. Nixon decided not to make Colvin the test case (the case used to challenge the law in court). She was young and became pregnant, and they judged that a respectable adult would command more support.

Bus boycotts had been tried elsewhere before, including in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 1953, which Montgomery's organisers knew of. Colvin and Smith later became plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal case that ended bus segregation.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Rosa Parks (arrested 1 December 1955), Claudette Colvin (March 1955) and Mary Louise Smith (October 1955). The WPC (Robinson), the NAACP (Nixon, Parks) and the MIA (King) are three different organisations.

notes.h: The arrest of Rosa Parks and the start of the boycott
notes.b: The arrest of Rosa Parks on 1 December 1955 gave the organisers the adult test case they wanted. A one-day protest then became a boycott lasting 381 days.
points: Parks was arrested on Thursday 1 December 1955 on a Cleveland Avenue bus, because she refused to give her seat to a white passenger when the driver, James F. Blake, demanded it.
Parks was no tired, accidental protester. She was a seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store and secretary of the Montgomery NAACP branch.
Parks had also investigated cases of sexual violence against black women for the NAACP, and in summer 1955 she attended a workshop at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee.

E. D. Nixon, president of the Montgomery NAACP branch and a Pullman porters' union leader, bailed her out with the help of the white couple Clifford and Virginia Durr. He backed using her case to challenge the law, and Fred Gray was her lawyer.
Parks was tried on 5 December 1955, found guilty of breaking the segregation law and given a small fine. Her case went on in the Alabama courts.

On the night of her arrest Robinson and the WPC, helped by students at Alabama State College, ran off tens of thousands of leaflets calling for a one-day boycott on Monday 5 December. Ministers announced it from their pulpits on Sunday 4 December, and the leaflets were handed out through churches and schools.
The one-day boycott was almost completely observed. That evening about 5,000 people at a mass meeting in the Holt Street Baptist Church voted to continue it.

The three demands were courteous treatment by drivers, seating first-come first-served (white from the front, black from the back), and black drivers on mainly black routes. They did not at first call for an end to segregation.
The city and bus company refused even these modest terms. This is why the demand grew into a demand for desegregation as the boycott went on.
notes.tip: Keep the dates in order: arrest 1 December, trial and first boycott day 5 December. The boycott was a one-day protest at first and became a 381-day campaign after the Holt Street vote. Examiners want the trigger (the arrest) kept separate from the causes.

notes.h: Organising the boycott: the MIA and its leaders
notes.b: A boycott of this size needed a leadership. The Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) was formed to run it, and it chose a young minister as its president.
points: The MIA was formed on 5 December 1955, and the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. was elected its president. He was 26, pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, and had arrived in Montgomery in 1954.
King was chosen partly because he was new in the city and had no record of conflict with the white authorities, so he had no enemies among the black leaders and was harder to attack.
At the Holt Street meeting King's address combined a demand for justice with a commitment to non-violence and Christian love. It launched him as the movement's voice.
Other leaders were Ralph Abernathy, E. D. Nixon and Jo Ann Robinson. The movement drew on the black churches, whose ministers were free from white employers' control.

Bayard Rustin, a pacifist and experienced organiser, and Glenn Smiley came to Montgomery in February 1956 to advise King on non-violence. The movement was told to stay disciplined in the face of attacks.
King later said that in January 1956, after threatening phone calls, he had prayed at his kitchen table and felt a sense of divine reassurance, which strengthened his resolve.
notes.tip: Say that King was the MIA's president but not the originator of the boycott, which was already under way. Never write that he began it.

notes.h: Organising the boycott: car pools, churches and economic pressure
notes.b: About 40,000 black bus riders stayed off the buses for more than a year. They could do this only because the churches and the car pool gave them another way to get to work.
points: The car pool was run by volunteers with several hundred cars and by black taxi drivers who charged the bus fare of ten cents. It took passengers to work and school, so people could keep their jobs while boycotting.
The MIA organised dispatch points at churches and a pick-up system, which is why the car pool ran like a transport service rather than an informal favour.
Churches raised money to buy station wagons for the car pool. Funds and support also came from northern supporters, unions and churches across the country.
Thousands of people walked, and many black domestic workers kept walking long distances to their jobs in white households. This showed the protest's determination.
The boycott hit the bus company's income hard, and city centre shops lost custom from black shoppers. The economic pressure on white Montgomery was therefore real.
notes.tip: 'How it was organised' answers need specifics: the MIA, the car pool with church dispatch points, ministers, WPC leaflets and mass meetings. 'They refused to ride the buses' is not enough.

notes.h: White resistance: harassment, violence and arrests
notes.b: Montgomery's white authorities tried to break the boycott by dividing its supporters, by harassment and arrests, and by violence.
points: The mayor and city commissioners announced falsely that the boycott had been settled, hoping to divide the boycotters. The police also arrested car pool drivers for minor offences and told taxi drivers to charge a higher minimum fare.
The White Citizens' Councils and the Ku Klux Klan threatened leaders. Employers dismissed black workers who took part, and the police harassed car pool drivers.
King was arrested on 26 January 1956 for driving 30 miles an hour in a 25 mile zone, a minor charge that showed the police were watching the leaders.

On 30 January 1956 a bomb was thrown on the porch of King's house while his wife Coretta and baby daughter were inside. Nobody was hurt, and King urged the angry crowd that gathered to go home and not retaliate.

In February 1956 a grand jury indicted 89 leaders of the boycott, including many ministers, under a 1921 Alabama law against boycotts. King was tried in March 1956 and convicted, fined 500 dollars, and the sentence was suspended pending appeal.
The indictments brought national press attention, and the images of ministers lining up to be booked turned the arrests into a symbol of dignity.
notes.tip: Say 'many ministers' rather than quoting a number of ministers indicted.

notes.h: The legal challenge: Browder v. Gayle
notes.b: While the boycott kept up economic pressure, a federal court case attacked segregation itself. This case, not Rosa Parks's, was what finally settled the matter.
points: On 1 February 1956 the lawyer Fred Gray filed Browder v. Gayle in the federal court for four black women: Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin and Mary Louise Smith. It challenged the constitutionality of bus segregation.
Rosa Parks was not a plaintiff (a person bringing a case), because her case was still in the Alabama courts and could have taken years. Her case did not go to the Supreme Court.
On 5 June 1956 a three-judge federal court ruled by two votes to one that bus segregation violated the Fourteenth Amendment, and the city and state appealed to the Supreme Court.
On 13 November 1956 the Supreme Court affirmed the decision, in a brief unsigned order relying on Brown v. Board of Education and later decisions. It denied a rehearing on 17 December.

On 13 November the city's lawyers also won a state court injunction (a court order) against the car pools as a public nuisance operating without a licence. King was in court for that hearing when reporters brought news of the Supreme Court ruling.
The formal Supreme Court order was served on Montgomery on 20 December 1956, and the MIA voted to end the boycott that day.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Browder v. Gayle (a federal case on buses, relying on Brown) with Brown v. Board of Education (schools, 1954). Only Colvin and Smith, not Parks, were plaintiffs in Browder.

notes.b: The boycott ended bus segregation in Montgomery after 381 days, from 5 December 1955 to 20 December 1956. Violence afterwards, and segregation elsewhere, limited what it changed.
points: The buses were desegregated on 21 December 1956, with King and Ralph Abernathy among the first to ride, in front of the press.
The MIA issued rules telling its members to be courteous, not to retaliate, and to sit anywhere without boasting.

Violence followed the victory. Snipers fired at buses in late December 1956, and the city suspended night bus service. On 10 January 1957 bombs damaged four black churches and the homes of Robert Graetz and Ralph Abernathy.
In January 1957 King and other ministers met in Atlanta to form a regional organisation, which was named the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) in August 1957, with King as president.
Segregation remained in Montgomery's schools, housing, restaurants and parks, and black voters were still largely excluded. The ruling covered buses only.
Parks lost her job and received threats, and she moved to Detroit in 1957.
notes.tip: The key dates for a document question are the order served on 20 December 1956, desegregated buses on 21 December 1956, the SCLC in 1957, and what stayed segregated. Use them to say how far the boycott brought change.

notes.h: The wider Alabama and Southern response, 1956
notes.b: The boycott provoked resistance across Alabama and the South. This shows how far white authorities would go to protect segregation.
points: The home of Robert Graetz, a white Lutheran minister serving a black congregation who supported the boycott, was bombed in August 1956.
Autherine Lucy was admitted to the University of Alabama in February 1956 but was suspended after white rioting and then expelled. This shows that the state's resistance went beyond the buses.
The state authorities banned the NAACP in Alabama in June 1956, which was designed to cut off the boycott's legal support. The Supreme Court overturned the ban in 1958.
The Southern Manifesto of March 1956 showed that most Southern members of Congress backed resistance to desegregation.
The violence did not break the boycott. National press coverage of the bombings and arrests brought sympathy from northern opinion and brought the matter to the federal courts.

notes.h: Key personality: Martin Luther King Jr. (role in the boycott)
notes.b: King led the boycott rather than started it, and Montgomery made him a national figure. Here we cover only his part in 1955 and 1956. There is more on this in the notes on racial conflict and the civil rights movement.
points: King was born in 1929, the son of a prominent Atlanta pastor, and gained a Boston University doctorate in 1955. He had been pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church only since 1954 when the boycott began.

As a direct participant he was elected MIA president on 5 December 1955, gave the Holt Street speech, led the car pool and its non-violent discipline, and was arrested, tried, and the target of a bomb. He was among the first to ride the desegregated bus, with Ralph Abernathy.
He was chosen partly because he was new and had no enemies, and Montgomery made him famous. He was a leader made by the boycott rather than its originator.

He shaped the boycott's tone by insisting on non-violence and on love for the opponent, based on Christian teaching and on Gandhi's methods, which he had studied and which Rustin and Smiley helped him apply during the boycott.
His memoir Stride Toward Freedom (1958) described the boycott and his thinking about non-violence.
Contemporaries in Montgomery's white leadership called him an outside agitator and tried to portray the boycott as run by communists. Black supporters saw him as an inspiring speaker and leader.
Historians such as Taylor Branch (Parting the Waters, 1988) emphasise King's growth into a national leader through Montgomery.
Aldon Morris (The Origins of the Civil Rights Movement, 1984) and others argue that local networks such as the churches existed before him. So King was a product as well as a maker of the movement.
notes.tip: Examiners want a balanced view: King's role (MIA president, Holt Street speech, non-violence, arrest, bomb) together with the point that he was a leader made by the boycott rather than its founder.

notes.h: Significance: King, non-violence and the movement
notes.b: Historians regard Montgomery as a model for the mass civil rights movement of the 1960s, though they disagree about how far it started that movement.
points: Non-violence became the movement's method. The boycott joined Christian ideas of love and forgiveness to Gandhi's methods of mass non-violent resistance.
It showed that black communities could organise sustained economic pressure on segregation, a method later used in sit-in campaigns.
It made the church the base of protest, and the MIA became a model for the SCLC. It also produced a national leader in King.
The role of women, including Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson and the WPC, was crucial, though men such as King and Nixon were more often given public recognition.
Jeanne Theoharis, in The Rebellious Life of Mrs Rosa Parks (2013), argues that the popular image of a tired seamstress acting on impulse hides Parks's long career as an activist.

Some historians argue that the courts, through Browder v. Gayle, which rested on Brown, rather than the boycott ended bus segregation. Others argue the boycott kept the case alive and made the ruling effective.
The boycott also gave the movement national and international publicity, which mattered in the Cold War, when the Soviet Union used American racism as propaganda.
notes.tip: Examiners reward a view on whether Montgomery was the start of the movement or one phase of a longer struggle, and on whether courts or protest caused the success. Give both sides, then your judgement.

notes.h: Assessment: how far did Montgomery bring change?
notes.b: Montgomery was a clear victory, but a limited one. Examiners reward answers that weigh achievements against limits and that compare how contemporaries and later historians judged it.
points: Achievement: Montgomery ended bus segregation in the city and defeated white resistance after 381 days, showing that organised, disciplined protest could defeat segregation.
Achievement: it produced a national leader, King, a lasting organisation, the SCLC, and a method of non-violent mass action later used in Birmingham and Selma.
Limit: the legal victory applied only to buses, so it did not change schools, housing, jobs or the voting restrictions in Alabama.

Limit: violence followed the victory, and white resistance across the South hardened after Brown and Montgomery, so real change came slowly until the Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Voting Rights Act 1965.
Contemporary white opinion in Montgomery condemned the boycott and used intimidation, while black residents who had endured segregation for decades saw the victory as a long overdue success.

Later historians stress the organisation the boycott created, the leaders it produced and the example it set. They debate whether it was the start of the civil rights movement or one phase of a longer struggle that began in the 1930s and 1940s.
notes.tip: In a document-based question, use the detail (dates, the ruling, the SCLC, what stayed segregated) to place the document and judge it. A balance of achievements and limits earns the top marks.

keyTerms.definition: The organisation formed on 5 December 1955 to co-ordinate the Montgomery bus boycott, with King as its president.
The unequal treatment of black Americans on Montgomery's buses, where segregation rules required them to give up seats to white passengers.
The federal case filed on 1 February 1956 challenging Montgomery's bus segregation, which the Supreme Court upheld on 13 November 1956.
The volunteer transport system that carried boycotting passengers to work and school in Montgomery during the boycott.
The Montgomery black women's organisation led by Jo Ann Robinson, which planned a bus boycott from 1954 and distributed its leaflets on 1 December 1955.
The strategy used in the Montgomery boycott of peaceful protest and refusal to comply with segregation, without retaliation against violence.
A network of white organisations founded in 1954 after Brown, which used economic and social pressure to defend segregation.
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, whose Montgomery branch was led by E. D. Nixon, with Rosa Parks as secretary.
